lesson.title: Paving the Nation: The Interstate Highway System
lesson.summary: The Federal Aid Highway Act of 1956 built the largest public works project in American history, reshaping where and how Americans lived and worked while also disrupting many existing communities.
lesson.body:
Two experiences shaped Dwight Eisenhower's thinking about American roads long before he became president. As a young Army officer in 1919, he took part in a transcontinental military convoy that took two months to cross the country on poor, often impassable roads. Decades later, as Supreme Allied Commander in Europe during World War II, he saw how Germany's Autobahn network let vehicles and troops move quickly across the country. Both experiences convinced him that the United States needed a modern highway system, partly for economic reasons and partly, in the language of the Cold War era he led as president, for national defense: fast roads could move troops and equipment, and could help evacuate cities in the event of a nuclear attack.

On June 29, 1956, Eisenhower signed the Federal Aid Highway Act, which created the National System of Interstate and Defense Highways. The federal government paid 90 percent of construction costs, funded by a dedicated Highway Trust Fund built from federal gasoline taxes, while states handled the remaining share and much of the planning. It was, by cost and scale, the largest public works project in American history, eventually growing to tens of thousands of miles of controlled access highway connecting nearly every major American city, built out gradually over several decades after 1956.

The interstate system reshaped American life in ways that went well beyond travel time. It made it far easier for families and businesses to move away from crowded city centers into new suburban developments, accelerating a suburbanization trend already underway. Trucking became a faster and cheaper way to move goods than railroads for many purposes, reshaping the national economy. Small towns that had once thrived on travelers passing along older highways, like the famous Route 66, often withered once the interstate routed traffic around them instead of through them.

The new highways also caused real harm in many cities, a fact that is essential to understanding their full history. Urban planners frequently routed interstate segments directly through existing neighborhoods, and because those neighborhoods often had little political power, the routes disproportionately cut through Black and other minority communities, destroying homes, businesses, and churches that had taken generations to build. Cities including Miami, New Orleans, and Detroit, among many others, saw thriving neighborhoods physically divided or leveled to make way for elevated freeways. The interstate system is remembered, accurately, as both an engineering triumph that connected the country and a policy whose costs fell unevenly on communities that had little say in the decision.
